results.title: Modern Methods to Measure Evapotranspiration in Commercial Agriculture
results.content: # Modern Methods to Measure Evapotranspiration in Commercial Agriculture. In many regions, abrupt changes to the climate have led to unexpected droughts and emphasized the importance of accurate measurement of evapotranspiration. These measurements inform decisions related to water resource management, wildfire prevention, the protection of endangered species, and agriculture. In particular, accurate measurements of evapotranspiration are critical for effective irrigation management, as most land precipitation is returned into the atmosphere through this process. New methods for measuring evapotranspiration have enabled farmers to prevent overwatering and more effectively respond to drought. Accurate measurements of evapotranspiration provide invaluable information for agricultural planning and irrigation systems. ## What are the methods of evapotranspiration measurement today? It can enable you to plan for your seasonal water needs, to some extent, but farmers utilizing this method are vulnerable to sudden changes in weather. A lysimeter is a large container installed within a field that attempts to measure evapotranspiration. An atmometer is a device that uses a ceramic plate connected to a water supply by a straw to measure evapotranspiration. As with the lysimeter, the more accurately the atmometer reflects the conditions of the plant, the better the measurement. It’s easy to measure evapotranspiration with an atmometer. You can either operate your own, manual atmometer, or purchase an electronic version, like ETGage, which will automatically read and log the rate of evapotranspiration as the water evaporates from the plate. ## How can machine learning improve evapotranspiration measurement? If you install an automated evapotranspiration system, machine learning can automatically analyze your data to provide more actionable information. While there is variance in evapotranspiration throughout a farm, machine learning can allow us to more accurately extrapolate forecasts over larger areas, reducing the up-front cost for functional evapotranspiration measurement. Benchmark Labs aggregates NWS and NOAA data alongside the data recorded by localized farm sensors to create personalized forecasting for evapotranspiration and other important measures. As the climate continues to change and droughts become a greater risk, better evapotranspiration measurement and localized weather modeling will enable farmers to protect their crops and improve the efficiency of their automated irrigation systems. Benchmark Labs is creating specialized machine learning models to create the world’s best evapotranspiration forecasting and localized 10-day forecasts.

results.title: Seasonal hysteresis of surface urban heat islands | PNAS
results.content: Temporal dynamics of urban warming have been extensively studied at the diurnal scale, but the impact of background climate on the observed seasonality of surface urban heat islands (SUHIs) remains largely unexplored. A coarse-grained model of SUHI coupled with a stochastic soil water balance is developed to demonstrate that the time lags between radiation forcing, air temperature, and rainfall generate a rate-dependent hysteresis, explaining the observed seasonal variations of . It is hypothesized here that this phenomenon is the result of time lags between the surface energy budget of cities, which is largely controlled by solar radiation, and the energy/water fluxes of rural areas, regulated by regional climate and vegetation seasonality (26–28). Specifically, a stochastic soil moisture balance is coupled with a coarse-grained SUHI model to demonstrate that the manifold of observed hysteretic seasonal patterns is encoded in the time lags between energy availability (radiation/temperature) and water availability (rainfall). To test the hypothesis that hysteresis is the result of time lags between urban and rural dynamics, we have modeled background meteorological forcings (i.e., incoming shortwave radiation , air temperature , wind speed , and rainfall frequency ) with sine functions characterized by mean , amplitude , and phase (*Materials and Methods*). Urban–rural surface temperature differences are regulated by urban-induced changes in evapotranspiration (), albedo (), convection efficiency (), surface emissivity (), and anthropogenic heat (), which vary with background climate and city characteristics (see *Materials and Methods* and *SI Appendix*, Figs. In general, the intensity of UHIs (both in terms of air and surface temperatures) is directly linked to local precipitation (15, 17, 18, 28), and urban cool islands generally occur in seasonally dry climates (15, 16, 73, 75) where sparse natural vegetation generates barren surfaces that have lower , sometimes lower albedo, and are less efficient in dissipating heat than 3D urban fabrics (15, 73, 76). In wet regions, the phase shift between radiation and temperature largely explains the seasonality of SUHIs, while in dry climates, hysteresis is further controlled by the intraannual variability of rainfall and its impact on soil moisture, background evapotranspiration, and albedo. * [e [...] changes in surface temperature caused by urbanization](#core-r18-5). * [e [...] changes in surface temperature caused by urbanization](#core-r18-5).

results.title: How Does Urban Density Affect Uhi? → Question
results.content: > Urban density significantly influences the Urban Heat Island effect by concentrating heat-absorbing surfaces and energy use. > The Urban Heat Island intensifies cooling energy demands in dense areas, creating a significant energy and sustainability challenge. Considering UHI effects during the design phase of new developments, especially in dense areas, can significantly reduce their contribution to the heat island and subsequent energy demand. Addressing UHI through thoughtful urban design and material choices becomes an integral part of reducing peak energy demand and building resilient, sustainable urban energy systems capable of handling future climate challenges. The core argument here, potentially controversial in simplistic narratives promoting density solely for transportation efficiency gains, posits that while density may offer certain energy advantages in mobility, its exacerbation of UHI imposes a significant, often underestimated, penalty on building energy consumption, particularly for cooling, thereby presenting a critical challenge to urban energy sustainability. Studies analyzing urban surface energy balance demonstrate how these materials significantly alter the partitioning of incoming solar radiation compared to vegetated surfaces where latent heat flux (evapotranspiration) dominates cooling. Anthropogenic Heat Release (AHR) in dense urban cores is a critical, often substantial, contributor to the UHI effect, particularly in temperate and cold climates during heating seasons, but increasingly dominant in all climates during peak cooling periods. > High urban density concentrates low-albedo surfaces and anthropogenic heat, exacerbating thermal stress and energy demand. The interaction between building-level, district-level, and grid-scale energy storage solutions presents a fertile area for research and application in high-density urban contexts facing significant UHI challenges. > Mitigating the Urban Heat Island in dense areas requires integrated strategies across urban planning, material science, and energy systems. Designing buildings and urban spaces to reduce heat gain in the first place, through optimized orientation, shading devices, natural ventilation strategies, and high-performance envelopes, can significantly reduce the reliance on energy-intensive mechanical cooling, thereby lowering AHR and mitigating the UHI effect.
